description: Measurable architecture properties, weights, and scoring rules for Enterprise Crypto-Agility evaluation.

OPTIMAL.label: Optimal Agility
OPTIMAL.description: Fully automated, modular, PQC-ready architecture with automated rollback and zero-downtime deployment.

HIGH.label: High Agility
HIGH.description: Strong provider abstractions, automated rotation pipelines, and hybrid-capable protocols.

MODERATE.label: Moderate Agility
MODERATE.description: Partial configuration centralization with manual migration and testing steps required.

LOW.label: Low Agility
LOW.description: High coupling, scattered hardcoded algorithms, high migration friction and manual certificate renewal.

RIGID.label: Rigid / Brittle
RIGID.description: Monolithic hardcoded algorithms, zero abstraction, static keys, and severe modernization blockers.

dimensions.name: Centralized Algorithm Configuration
dimensions.description: Degree to which cryptographic algorithms, key sizes, and cipher parameters are managed through centralized external configuration rather than hardcoded code literals.

positive_signals.description: Algorithms and ciphers loaded from dedicated policy configuration files (e.g. YAML, JSON, Consul, or Vault).
Single central registry or module encapsulating algorithm parameters across the service.
Cipher suite selection configurable at deployment time via environment variables.

negative_signals.description: Raw algorithm name strings (e.g. 'RSA', 'AES-256-CBC') hardcoded directly in application business logic.
Multiple discordant cipher definitions distributed across > 5 independent source files.
Hardcoded numeric constants used for key lengths or buffer allocations.

dimensions.name: Replaceability
dimensions.description: Ease of substituting cryptographic algorithms via modular design, interfaces, and strategy patterns without modifying caller code.

positive_signals.description: Application business logic consumes abstract interfaces or base classes rather than concrete cipher implementations.
Factory or dependency injection container manages cryptographic primitive instantiation.
Cryptographic payloads include algorithm identifier metadata headers enabling multi-algorithm parsing.

negative_signals.description: Direct instantiation of concrete crypto classes (e.g. new RSACryptoServiceProvider()) in controller/service layers.
Buffer sizes statically fixed to classical signature sizes (e.g. 256 or 512 bytes), which breaks on PQC signatures.
Wire format or database schema tied to algorithm-specific binary representations.

dimensions.name: Key Lifecycle Management
dimensions.description: Maturity of automated key generation, rotation, expiration tracking, and hardware/KMS integration.

positive_signals.description: Private and master keys managed within certified cloud KMS or Hardware Security Modules (FIPS 140-2/3).
Periodic automated rotation enabled with seamless dual-decryption / previous-key verification support.
Communication protocols enforce ephemeral forward secrecy (PFS) for every session.

negative_signals.description: Symmetric keys, private keys, or API secrets hardcoded in source code or static configuration.
Keys configured without expiration dates or rotation tracking policies.
Stateful hash signatures (LMS/XMSS) utilized without non-volatile monotonic hardware counter protection.

dimensions.name: Protocol Agility
dimensions.description: Ability to negotiate modern cryptographic protocols and dynamically adapt cipher suite groups without recompilation.

positive_signals.description: TLS 1.3 enabled with runtime-configurable key exchange groups and modern ALPN negotiation.
Graceful client-server protocol negotiation with strict minimum version enforcement.
Support for standard protocol extensions (e.g. supported_groups, key_share, signature_algorithms).

negative_signals.description: Enforcement or hardcoding of legacy insecure protocols (TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, SSLv3).
Static cipher list hardcoded in application binary preventing group negotiation updates.
Protocol negotiation extensions disabled or bypassed.

dimensions.name: Certificate Automation
dimensions.description: Automation of certificate issuance, enrollment, renewal, validation, and revocation.

positive_signals.description: ACME protocol or automated CA enrollment pipeline handling automated renewal.
Certificate lifetimes <= 90 days, reducing vulnerability exposure window.
OCSP stapling and automated revocation checks active in production endpoints.

negative_signals.description: Certificates manually copied or uploaded to servers without automation.
Active certificates found expired or expiring within 14 days without active renewal pipeline.
Self-signed certificates in production without enterprise PKI governance.

dimensions.name: Provider Abstraction
dimensions.description: Decoupling from proprietary or vendor-specific cryptographic APIs through standardized provider architectures.

positive_signals.description: Uses standard provider architectures (Java JCA/JCE, WebCrypto API, OpenSSL 3.x Providers, Go standard crypto).
Hardware interactions abstracted via PKCS#11, Microsoft CNG, or cloud provider KMS abstractions.
Repository maintains an internal adapter layer shielding core code from external library changes.

negative_signals.description: Direct invocation of non-standard proprietary cryptographic SDKs or vendor-locked hardware APIs.
Direct access to low-level internal structs or unabstracted C memory pointers in application code.

dimensions.name: Dependency Coupling
dimensions.description: Containment of cryptographic dependencies and minimization of blast radius across application code.

positive_signals.description: All cryptographic operations encapsulated in a dedicated internal microservice or isolated package.
Cryptographic dependencies consumed in <= 2 internal modules (blast radius <= 2).
All crypto library dependencies pinned, vulnerability-scanned, and actively maintained.

negative_signals.description: Cryptographic library symbols imported and invoked directly in >= 5 disparate business logic modules.
Repository imports multiple overlapping crypto libraries (e.g. BouncyCastle + raw WebCrypto + forge).

dimensions.name: Test Coverage
dimensions.description: Completeness of automated cryptographic testing including CAVP/KAT vectors, downgrade resilience, and regression suites.

positive_signals.description: Cryptographic implementations verified against NIST CAVP / RFC Known Answer Tests (KAT).
Automated tests verify that client/server rejects cipher and protocol downgrade attacks.
Integration tests verify end-to-end data processing when algorithm configuration is toggled.

negative_signals.description: No unit, integration, or regression tests covering cryptographic operations.
Tests only mock cryptographic primitives and never execute actual encryption/signing logic.

dimensions.name: PQC / Hybrid Readiness
dimensions.description: Architectural preparedness for Post-Quantum Cryptography including hybrid key exchange, composite signatures, and buffer tolerances.

positive_signals.description: Dependencies include PQC-enabled stacks (OpenSSL 3.4+, liboqs, Bouncy Castle 1.78+, BoringSSL).
Architecture supports hybrid groups (e.g. X25519MLKEM768) combining classical and quantum-safe key exchange.
Data structures, network MTUs, and serialization accommodate larger PQC keys and signatures (> 1500B).

negative_signals.description: Packet sizes or database schemas strictly capped at classical sizes, failing on PQC key shares.
Core dependency on legacy crypto libraries that have ceased development without PQC plans.

dimensions.name: Rollback Capability
dimensions.description: Operational capability to perform zero-downtime, automated rollbacks of cryptographic changes during production failures.

positive_signals.description: Algorithm and cipher suite selection controllable via dynamic feature flags or proxy toggles.
Dual-stack verification or dual-decryption compatibility enabled during migration transitions.
Monitoring alerts (handshake error rate, P99 latency) trigger automated circuit breakers.

negative_signals.description: One-way data re-encryption or key destruction without rollback failover capability.
Rollback requires full service redeployment or downtime rather than dynamic reconfiguration.
